claims.text: Thermomechanical processing can be used to improve phase stability, refine microstructure, and optimize properties in HEAs and RHEAs.
Hot rolling, forging, and heat treatment are applicable thermomechanical processing techniques for the stated HEA and RHEA objective.
Thermomechanical processing requires controlled temperature, pressure, and deformation conditions.
The conditions used in high-pressure synchrotron XRD experiments are examples of relevant thermomechanical processing conditions.
Grain size, grain boundaries, and precipitate formation are structural mediators of the proposed processing effects.
Milling time and mechanical alloying influence grain size, grain boundaries, and precipitate formation.
Thermomechanical processing acts through recrystallization, grain growth, and precipitation hardening.
Recrystallization, grain growth, and precipitation hardening can improve phase stability.
Recrystallization, grain growth, and precipitation hardening can refine microstructure.
Recrystallization, grain growth, and precipitation hardening can optimize strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance.
Some RHEAs combine relatively low density with high strength at elevated temperatures.
RHEAs can exhibit good phase stability at high temperatures.
Thermomechanical processing can improve an as-cast or wrought baseline microstructure and its properties.
Maximum processing temperature and deformation strain can affect the final microstructure and properties.
The outcome depends on the particular material, processing conditions, and desired properties.
Adding antioxidant alloying elements can improve oxidation resistance.
Processed samples can be compared with as-cast or wrought controls using XRD, SEM, mechanical testing, and corrosion measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if thermomechanical processing produces no significant improvement in phase stability, microstructure refinement, or property optimization.
